title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The preregistered primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task, reused across arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report every paired episode as safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Because shared_initial_candidate semantics produced identical shared candidates that passed deterministic validation for every task, no validator‑triggered repairs occurred and the paired contrast is uninformative in this run. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, analysis results, a mechanistic explanation for the null paired outcome, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating translation from high‑level operator intent to concrete device configurations is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows can produce configuration sequences, but token‑level or text‑similarity metrics fail to capture ordering, dependency, invariants, and transient states that determine whether a configuration is safe to apply. Executable, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configs are applied to device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient invariant violations, protected‑resource touches) that text‑only tests miss.

A recurring architectural pattern to improve safety is generate–validate–repair (GVR): (i) an LLM generates a candidate configuration; (ii) a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants; (iii) an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate if violations are detected. Prior work reports GVR‑style gains on many syntactic and some semantic faults, but key empirical questions remain about whether deterministic verifiers reduce unsafe application rates under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and how experimental design choices (notably paired generation semantics) affect the ability to measure verifier benefit.

Research question and contributions. After a fresh literature review and a preregistered experimental plan, we asked: Does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a GVR pipeline reduce the paired unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) for LLM‑generated configurations under matched in‑distribution, distribution‑shift, and adversarial conditions when executed in a paired, emulation‑grounded benchmark? Our contributions are: (1) a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded execution (N=240 pairs) that adheres to the registered shared_initial_candidate semantics; (2) an artifact‑grounded mapping from the preregistered estimand to archived analysis outputs, and exact quantitative results (paired difference, bootstrap CI, McNemar p); and (3) a focused failure analysis showing why the paired contrast was null in this run and recommendations—grounded in archived execution accounting—for future informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Emulation‑grounded benchmarks for LLM agents in NetOps have recently been proposed to surface workflow and planning faults beyond textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this executable closed‑loop approach. Work on configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators can enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, with effectiveness depending on verifier coverage and repair search strategy. Surveys and position pieces synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising directions for operational NetOps safety. Engineering precedent from mature configuration-analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) informs verifier design and incremental verification practices.

Our study differs in three ways: (a) it preregistered a single, precisely defined paired estimand and execution semantics; (b) it used shared_initial_candidate execution semantics (one initial generation per task reused across arms), which constrains the possible paired outcomes; and (c) it archives per‑call traces, deterministic validation traces, and analysis artifacts so the numeric estimand and its provenance are directly reconcilable to the artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 if a final configuration would produce a semantic safety violation when executed in the emulator, and safe_apply = 0 otherwise. The preregistration specified a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produces exactly one initial LLM generation per task, and both arms reuse that shared candidate; the guarded arm may request up to one validator‑triggered repair. Under that contract, the guarded arm can only produce a different final result than baseline if the shared candidate fails validation and a repair is applied.

Design, tasks, and sampling. We executed N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks, deterministically generated and blocked into topology/vendor clusters. Task mix: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Adversarial prompts were generated under the preregistered fixed‑seed adversary protocol to produce a blinded adversarial subset. Inclusion/exclusion and retry rules: up to two infra retries for technical failures; pairs with unrecoverable infra failure were to be excluded from primary analysis (none occurred).

Model, adapter, and verifier contract. Execution declared the hosted model gpt-5-mini. The adapter family implements the shared_initial_candidate contract (one shared initial generation per task). The guarded pipeline used a deterministic network validator that checks semantic invariants and, when violations are detected, may invoke a single automated repair attempt per task. The verifier decision is binary for the estimand (final configuration passes or fails semantic checks); repair prompts and any edits are recorded for analysis when applied.

Scoring and analysis mapping. Final outcome per episode is binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by emulator execution and deterministic validation. The preregistered primary analysis executor computed the paired contingency table, a bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples), and an exact McNemar two‑sided p‑value on discordant pairs. Archive artifacts used for reporting include the condition summary and paired contingency artifacts produced by the analysis executor; bootstrap parameters (resamples and seed) are recorded in the analysis log. Sensitivity channels for planned exclusions (e.g., validator PASS vs emulator mismatch) were declared; items flagged under those channels would be treated in predeclared sensitivity analyses.

Execution controls and reproducibility. All model‑call metadata, task manifests, validator traces, and final scored outputs were archived in the execution bundle to enable deterministic reconciliation of the reported numeric outputs with archived artifacts. The shared_initial_candidate semantics constrained provider call accounting to one initial model call per task and thereby limited generator variability across conditions by design.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run completed according to the preregistered plan: planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240. Provider call accounting recorded exactly one initial model generation per task (model calls used = 240), consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. No infra failures, no unscorable episodes, and no preregistered exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency. Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Condition summaries show baseline successes = 240/240 and guarded successes = 240/240. The paired contingency table is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. Consequently the paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All analysis artifacts referenced in these statements are archived in the execution bundle produced by the registered analysis executor.

Validator activity and repair usage. No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode; repair attempt counts are zero across the archived repair logs. Representative validator traces record validator PASS on the shared initial candidates and document observed command counts and difficulty labels for inspected tasks. Because the guarded final outputs matched the shared initial candidate in every episode, baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across the full task set and within subgroups (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial), yielding degenerate subgroup contrasts.

Planned sensitivity channels not invoked. The preregistration specified sensitivity analyses to handle 'possible false‑safe' flags (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra failures; none were triggered, so all planned sensitivity channels remain unused for this run. The planning artifacts and the contingency artifacts necessary to run those sensitivity analyses are archived for future reanalysis under alternative assumptions.
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation for the null paired contrast. The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one shared LLM output per task and both arms reused that candidate. Deterministic validation passed every shared candidate; under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only alter the paired outcome by invoking a repair when validation failed. Because no shared candidate failed validation, no repairs were invoked and no discordant pairs occurred. This mechanistic account—grounded in provider call counts and validator records—fully explains the degenerate paired contingency (estimate=0.0; CI=[0.0,0.0]; p=1.0).

Design tradeoffs and implications. Shared_initial_candidate semantics reduces model‑call budget and guarantees a direct pairing of generator output across conditions, simplifying paired estimand interpretation when generator variance is a nuisance. However, it also constrains the experiment: verifier benefit can be observed only when the single shared generation fails validation. To causally estimate verifier effect as an intervention on the generation→application pipeline, experimenters should consider alternative designs: (A) independent initial generations per arm so generator variability is part of the causal contrast; (B) intentionally introduce generator perturbations or stronger adversaries to increase the probability of initial candidate failure; or (C) increase repair budget (allow multiple repair iterations) so repair behavior can be exercised and measured. Each option has tradeoffs in model‑call budget, interpretability, and operational realism.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared_initial_candidate contract is an explicit design choice that restricts the causal interpretation of the paired contrast; archived provider accounting demonstrates adherence to that contract. Construct validity: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of semantic checks; while validator traces show detailed recording of observed fields and violation codes, unmeasured semantic fault classes may remain. External validity: tasks derive from a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus and a deterministic task generator; extrapolation to production, multi‑vendor deployments and operator workflows requires caution. Conclusion validity: realized baseline unsafe rate = 0 prevents detection of verifier benefit given this design; powering future experiments to observe informative discordant pairs requires design changes that increase initial candidate failure probability.

Artifact‑grounded recommendations. (1) If the objective is to measure verifier causal impact, avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or include independent generation for at least one arm. (2) Increase the repair budget and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior and resultant quality changes. (3) Strengthen adversary protocols (beyond a single fixed seed) to probe adaptive prompt manipulations reproducibly. (4) Expand verifier coverage and add cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect false‑safe behavior; automate diagnostic flags and archive them for sensitivity analysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms, yielding a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). The null paired result is mechanistically explained by the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract: with a single shared initial generation per task that passed deterministic validation in every case, the guarded arm had no opportunity to apply repairs and therefore could not produce discordant outcomes. We present this artifact‑grounded execution and analysis so that future studies can adopt alternative generation semantics, stronger adversaries, or expanded repair budgets to yield informative paired contrasts about verifier value in operational NetOps settings.

disclosure_statement: Execution used a single hosted model (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini") via the registered adapter family (hosted_netops_gvr_v1). The guarded pipeline used a deterministic network validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. The study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen preregistered plan after the autonomy lock. The registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); under that contract a paired divergence could occur only if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the autonomy lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. The immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Execution artifacts (preregistration and the archived execution and analysis bundle) are available in the run archive referenced by the study identifier; these artifacts contain the per‑call traces, task manifests, validator traces, and analysis outputs that substantiate the numeric results reported above. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and made verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
